title: Occasion: the Lane gallery and Dublin in 1913
short: Published in the Irish Times, 8 September 1913, as 'Romance in Ireland (On reading much of the correspondence against the Art Gallery)'.
body: The poem attacks the Dublin middle class who opposed building a municipal gallery for Sir Hugh Lane's collection of modern French paintings. In his note of 1914 Yeats listed this as the third of three controversies (after the Parnell split and The Playboy riots) that showed Irish minds without culture, and named William Martin Murphy, organiser of the lock-out then in progress, as a leader of the opposition. The title it now bears gives the month of the Lockout, which had begun in August 1913, but the poem was not written about the strike. Reprinted as 'Romantic Ireland' in 1914, it took its present title only in the 1916 edition of Responsibilities. The opening question is scornful: 'being come to sense' mocks the prudence of people who think they have grown up.

title: fumble in a greasy till
short: The shopkeeper's cash-drawer, handled with greasy fingers: Yeats's image of the new Catholic middle class.
body: The till is a cash drawer; 'fumble' and 'greasy' make the getting of money furtive and dirty. Yeats associated this class with the Irish 'Paudeen', the name he gives the huckster in a neighbouring poem, and in his 1914 note he blames the rise of 'our new middle class' for the baseness he saw in Dublin's public quarrels. Critics have pointed out the social snobbery of the attack, made by a Protestant poet against Catholic tradesmen, and the poem is also read alongside the Lockout, though Yeats did not write it about the strike.

title: And prayer to shivering prayer
short: Prayers counted up like coins: a piety of accumulation and fear rather than generosity.
body: The zeugma ('add the halfpence to the pence / And prayer to shivering prayer') puts money and prayer in the same ledger. 'Shivering' suggests fearful, cold devotion. Yeats's 1914 note complains that religious Ireland thinks of divine things 'as a round of duties separated from life', which is exactly the habit the line satirises. The phrase 'For men were born to pray and save' is the mercantile creed put in ironic aphorism.

anchor: dried the marrow from the bone
title: dried the marrow from the bone
short: Until all vitality is gone: thrift and fearful piety leave nothing living.
body: Marrow is the living substance inside bones and, proverbially, the core of strength and vigour. To dry it is to reduce life to a dead skeleton. The line marks the end of the first sentence's long movement and sets up the refrain's verdict that the romantic, self-sacrificing Ireland is dead. There may also be an echo of the biblical 'dry bones' (Ezekiel 37), a valley of bones without life, though Yeats's image is domestic and commercial rather than prophetic. The verb 'dried' makes the process slow and deliberate, the work of a lifetime of saving.

title: The refrain
short: Repeated at the end of each stanza, then altered in the last; Yeats later said it 'sounds old-fashioned now'.
body: Each eight-line stanza of iambic tetrameter (rhymed ababcdcd) closes with the same couplet, a ballad device that gives the satire the cadence of a lament. In the last stanza the refrain changes to 'But let them be, they're dead and gone, / They're with O'Leary in the grave', shifting from the dead idea to the dead men. In a note dated July 1916 Yeats wrote that the refrain had seemed true in 1913 but that he 'did not foresee 1916': the Easter Rising proved romantic Ireland alive, a reversal he explored in 'Easter, 1916'.

title: O'Leary
short: John O'Leary (1830-1907), Fenian leader, imprisoned and exiled, who became Yeats's mentor in Dublin.
body: O'Leary was a leader of the Irish Republican Brotherhood, convicted in 1865 and imprisoned, then exiled; he returned to Dublin in 1885 and became the young Yeats's guide, lending him books of Irish poetry and modelling a nationalism of honour rather than self-interest. He died on 16 March 1907. For Yeats he embodied an aristocratic, disinterested patriotism, which the poem contrasts with shopkeeping prudence.

anchor: names that stilled your childish play
title: The names that stilled your childish play
short: The heroes whose names, told in childhood, once silenced children with awe.
body: The line recalls a time when the names of rebels were spoken with reverence at home, enough to stop children's games. The irony is that the same people, grown up and 'come to sense', now prize money and prayer. The heroes 'have gone about the world like wind', scattered in exile and death and as hard to hold as air.

title: the hangman's rope
short: The fate of many rebels, most famously Robert Emmet, hanged in 1803.
body: The line imagines the rope spun in advance for the patriots, a fate they accepted. Unlike the shopkeepers, they had 'little time ... to pray', and nothing to 'save' in either sense (money or their lives). The play on 'save' links this stanza to the first, where men 'were born to pray and save'. The passive construction ('was spun') suggests a fate prepared by others, by the authorities who executed rebels, and accepted by the patriots as part of their calling.

title: the wild geese
short: The Irish soldiers who left for Continental armies after the Treaty of Limerick (1691), and their successors.
body: After the defeat of the Jacobite cause in 1691 thousands of Irish soldiers sailed for France and later served in the armies of France, Spain and Austria; they were called the Wild Geese, and the name was extended to later Irish exiles in foreign service. Yeats's image ('spread / The grey wing upon every tide') makes them migrating birds. The question 'Was it for this ...?' is a classical rhetorical form of indignation, implying that their sacrifice has been betrayed.

title: Edward Fitzgerald
short: Lord Edward FitzGerald (1763-1798), aristocratic leader of the United Irishmen, who died of wounds in Newgate.
body: A son of the Duke of Leinster and a former British army officer, Lord Edward joined the United Irishmen and was a principal planner of the 1798 rising. He was wounded while resisting arrest in May 1798 and died in Newgate Prison, Dublin, on 4 June. His noble birth made him for Yeats a type of the aristocratic patriot, which matters to the poem's contrast between generous gentry and calculating tradesmen.

title: Robert Emmet
short: Robert Emmet (1778-1803), leader of the failed rising of July 1803, hanged in Dublin in September 1803.
body: Emmet's rising in Dublin collapsed in a night; he was captured, tried and hanged in Thomas Street. His speech from the dock, asking that no man write his epitaph until Ireland took her place among the nations, made him the most romantic of Irish martyrs, celebrated by Thomas Moore among others. He is one of the patriots for whom 'the hangman's rope was spun'.

title: Wolfe Tone
short: Theobald Wolfe Tone (1763-1798), founder of the United Irishmen, who brought French help and died in prison in 1798.
body: Tone, a Protestant Dublin lawyer, helped found the Society of United Irishmen in 1791 and sought French military aid; he sailed with French expeditions in 1796 and 1798. Captured in November 1798 and sentenced to death, he died of a self-inflicted wound before execution. With Fitzgerald and Emmet he completes a trio of mostly Protestant, eighteenth-century republican heroes, which suited Yeats's picture of a lost, generous Ireland.

anchor: All that delirium of the brave
title: All that delirium of the brave
greek: Latin delirare, 'to leave the furrow', to be deranged
short: Heroism seen as a kind of noble madness, beyond the reckoning of prudent minds.
body: 'Delirium' (Latin delirare, to go out of the furrow) is a fever of the mind. Yeats calls the rebels' courage a delirium partly in admiration and partly to anticipate how the prudent would describe it. The phrase looks forward to the last stanza, where the shopkeepers would say a woman's hair had 'maddened every mother's son'. The phrase also has an elegiac grandeur: the rebels of 1798 and 1803 failed, but their failure is given the dignity of passion rather than error.

title: some woman's yellow hair
short: The prudent would dismiss the exiles' sacrifice as madness over a woman: readings differ over whether the woman is a lover, Ireland, or Helen.
body: If the dead returned, says the poem, the modern Dubliner would explain their loneliness and pain as infatuation, as if all of them had been driven mad by 'some woman's yellow hair'. Readers differ about the force of the image. It can be the shopkeepers' cynical reduction of patriotism to romance; it can also allude to the tradition, which Yeats used in his play Cathleen ni Houlihan (1902), of Ireland figured as a woman for whom young men die; and some hear an echo of Helen of Troy, for whose beauty a war was fought. The irony is that the dismissive phrase is, in a sense, true.

anchor: weighed so lightly what they gave
title: They weighed so lightly what they gave
short: The heroes did not calculate the cost of their sacrifice; the line Yeats quoted in 1916 about the Easter rebels.
body: 'Weighed' continues the commercial vocabulary of the first stanza: the shopkeepers weigh and count, the heroes gave without weighing. In his note of July 1916 Yeats quoted this line in praise of the leaders of the Easter Rising, who gave, 'in some cases without hope of success'. The line therefore turned out to describe heroes Yeats thought did not exist, and the poem's despair was overtaken within three years.
